Arc 10 covered Days 64–70 of Epoch 3, and it was all about Program Derived Addresses.
Arc 9 gave us our first Solana program.
We built a counter, stored its state in an account, restricted updates to the correct authority, and used LiteSVM to prove those rules worked.
But the counter account had a limitation.
It used a randomly generated keypair for its address.
That is manageable in a small exercise. The client creates the account, keeps hold of its public key, and passes that address back whenever it wants to increment the counter.
It becomes awkward once we want one counter per user.
Where do we store all those addresses? How does a user find their counter from another device? How does the program know that the account it received is the correct counter for that wallet?
Arc 10 answered …

articles.author: Tanmay Patwary
articles.description:
We built OpenScOut because finding a good open-source project shouldn't be harder than contributing to one


If you've ever tried to make your first (or fiftieth) open-source contribution, you know the drill.
You find a repository that looks interesting.
You open the issues tab hoping for a "good first issue."
The last commit was over a year ago.
The maintainer hasn't responded in months.
You close the tab and go back to scrolling GitHub.
After a while, "I'll contribute to open source someday" quietly becomes another unfinished goal.
We got tired of that experience, so we started building OpenScOut—a platform that helps developers discover active, beginner-friendly, and well-maintained open-source projects.
Finding a project isn't difficult.
Finding one that's active, welcoming, and worth investing your time in is.
Most developers only realize a repository is inactive after they've already spent time understanding the codebase.
Search repositories using filters like language, stars, forks, and recent activity to find projects that match your skills.
Analyze any GitHub repository and receive an A–F contribution readiness score based on project health, maintainer responsiveness, issue quality, activity, and more.
Browse Google Summer of Code organizations and project ideas from one place instead of jumping across multiple websites.
We believe developers should spend more time building and contributing than deciding whether a repository is worth contributing to.
OpenScOut is still in active development, and we're building it alongside the community. If you've ever struggled to find the right open-source project, we'd love your feedback.
We'll be sharing development updates, new features, and the launch over on LinkedIn.
👉 Follow the journey here:
Follow OpenScOut on LinkedIn
If you have ideas, feature requests, or want early access, leave a comment below—we'd love to hear from you.
Building in public, one repo at a time. 🚀
articles.title: We built an AI-powered scout for open source. Meet OpenScOut.

articles.description:
In CUDA programs, you can place only the GPU kernels in .cu files while keeping the rest of your code in .cpp files.
This organization confines CUDA-specific code to a limited set of files, making the overall program easier to maintain and understand.
This example uses the following two files:
kernel.cu
main.cpp

kernel.cu: Defines the CUDA kernel.
main.cpp: Launches the kernel and handles error checking.
In kernel.cu, define only the kernel that runs on the GPU.
__global__ void noopKernel()
{
    // A kernel that does nothing
}

A function marked with __global__ is launched from the CPU and executed on the GPU.
The noopKernel in this example performs no work. It is the smallest possible example for verifying that a kernel can be separated into its own file and launched successfully.
In ma…
articles.title: Separating Only CUDA Kernels into `.cu` Files

The 3am page that defines your career


At 3am, an availability zone goes dark. If your system is well-designed, nothing happens, traffic shifts, replicas take over, and you sleep through it. articles.author: Albert zhang
articles.description:
In a single-agent system, failure is simple: the agent errors, you retry.
In multi-agent systems, failure is a graph problem.
Agent A: ✅ Success
Agent B: ❌ Timeout (depends on A)
Agent C: ❌ Skipped (depends on B)
Agent D: ❌ Partial data (depends on C)

One timeout propagates through the entire pipeline. Without recovery, your system is fragile.
AgentForge implements 3 recovery layers:
@retry(max_attempts=3, backoff=exponential(base=2, max=60))
def agent_call(params):
    return llm.invoke(params)

If an agent fails 5 times in 10 minutes, we stop calling it and return a degraded response:
{
  "status": "degraded",
  "agent": "market_data",
  "fallback": "cached_data",
  "warning": "Real-time data unavailable, using 15-min delayed feed"
}

When a critical agent fails, the orchestrator can re-plan:
Skip the failed step if non-critical
Substitute with a backup agent
Halt and alert with full context trace
Last month, our market data API went down during trading hours. Here's what happened:
14:32 — Market data agent timeout (Layer 1: 3 retries failed)
14:33 — Circuit breaker opened for market data agent
14:33 — Pipeline automatically switched to cached data + warning flag
14:35 — Full report generated with "delayed data" disclaimer
15:00 — Market data API recovered, circuit breaker closed automatically
Zero manual intervention. Zero missed reports.
If your multi-agent system can't handle one agent failing, it's not production-ready.
AgentForge makes this the default, not an afterthought.
https://github.com/agentforge-cyber/agentforge-mvp
Posted on 2026-07-16 by the AgentForge team.
articles.title: Automatic Error Recovery in AI Agent Networks
